title: Similitude 9.16: The stones from the deep and the seal
sum: Hermas asks why the stones from the deep, the righteous who died before Christ, still had to come up through the water. The Shepherd answers that no one can enter the kingdom of God without putting off the deadness of the old life, and 'the seal is the water': people go down into it dead and come up alive (93:2-4). Even the forty, the apostles and teachers who already had the seal, came up from the deep, because after their own deaths they preached to those who had died before them and gave them the seal of the preaching (93:5-7).
Here the book says outright that the seal is baptism: 'the seal is the water' (93:4). Clement of Alexandria quoted the passage twice (Stromata 2.9 and 6.6).
readings: Hermas makes baptism necessary for everyone, even the righteous of old: no one enters the kingdom without the water. The point is the seal, not the dead as such; the dead are the hardest case, and Hermas solves it by sending the apostles to them.
Read as a picture of the descent to the dead

Others read the chapter beside 1 Peter 3:19 and 4:6 and the later belief that Christ went to the dead. Lake notes that it is 'more usually the Christ himself who descends to Hades for the purpose'. Hermas's version, with apostles who have died, may reflect a time before the belief took its later shape, or simply his own way of telling it.

views.H: Lake restores two short passages from the Latin and Ethiopic (93:3) and from Clement of Alexandria's quotation (93:6), where the Athos manuscript has skipped words; Clement's quotation shows that the sentence of 93:6 stood in his copy. The numbers of the stones from the deep (ten, twenty-five, thirty-five, forty in 92:4) do not match the parable's twenty in 81:3, and Lake says no explanation has been found.
views.N: John 3:5 (Lake's margin) stands behind 'enter the kingdom of God' and the need for water. 1 Peter 3:19 and 4:6 speak of preaching to the dead; Hermas gives the preaching to the apostles. Romans 6:3-4 has the same going down and coming up. What 1 Corinthians 15:29, baptism 'for the dead', meant is disputed (the site's card at 1 Corinthians 15); Hermas does not cite it.
views.D: Hermas's words 'the seal is the water' stand behind later talk of baptism as a seal. Whether baptism is necessary for salvation (Mark 16:16), whether God saves through the act (1 Peter 3:21), and what Christ did among the dead (1 Peter 3:19) are the site's cards; Hermas belongs to none of the later positions, but each side has read him.

deep.h: The apostles preach to the dead
deep.b:
Three things in this chapter have no clear parallel in the New Testament. First, the preachers are the apostles and teachers, not Christ. Second, they preach after their own deaths: they 'fell asleep in the power and faith of the Son of God' and then preached (93:5). Third, they baptize the dead: 'they went down into the water with them and came up again' (93:6). The forty already had the seal, so for them the going down and coming up was not a new birth: 'these went down alive and came up alive' (93:6).

Lake's footnote compares 1 Peter 3:19, the Gospel of Peter and the descent to the dead in the Acts of Pilate. In the Gospel of Peter a voice from heaven says to the risen Lord, 'You have preached to them that sleep', and the cross answers 'Yea' (section 10 in the New Advent English). Hermas's picture differs: the gospel reaches the dead through the same people who preached it to the living, and in the same way, by preaching and the seal.

Hermas does not say where the dead are, and the word Hades does not appear. He does not say how water can be used among the dead; the parable's 'deep' and the explanation's 'water' are one image. Clement of Alexandria (Stromata 2.9, ANF English) cites the passage for 'certain righteous among Gentiles and Jews' who had died before the preaching reached them. On the site, the whole question is gathered on the topic pages for the descent to the dead and for baptism for the dead.

deep.title: Claude's theory: why the apostles, not Christ?
deep.b: A guess, not a finding. Hermas never names Jesus in the whole book, and Christ only once (6:8), as a script search of Lake's Greek and Latin shows. His Son of God acts through others: the six glorious angels build the tower, the virgins carry the stones, the Shepherd teaches. Sending the apostles to the dead fits that pattern. The forty are already part of the tower's foundation (81:3), and in the parable everything that enters the tower comes through the gate, the Son of God (89:4-6). So the apostles bring the dead to the gate rather than the gate going to the dead. I have not found this argument in a source I opened; it rests on 81:3, 89:4-8 and 93:5-7.

echoes: John 3:5; Romans 6:3-4; 1 Peter 3:19; 1 Peter 4:6; Ephesians 4:9; Hebrews 11:39-40; 1 Corinthians 15:29; Ephesians 1:13

settings.what: The meaning of the stones from the deep
settings.by: The Shepherd, the angel of repentance, explaining the parable
settings.to: Hermas, in Arcadia beside the finished tower (78:4), asking question after question
settings.when: After the Shepherd has named the virgins, the women in black and the four groups of stones from the deep (92:1-6)
settings.why: To answer the hardest question the parable raises: how people who died before the gospel could be in the church. The answer makes baptism, 'the seal', the one way into the kingdom for everyone, and so raises the stakes for the hearers who have received it.
settings.readers: The Roman church that heard the book read (8:3) likely had members who asked about parents and ancestors who died before the gospel came; Clement of Alexandria used the passage that way, for 'certain righteous among Gentiles and Jews' (Stromata 2.9).

title: Similitude 9.17: The twelve mountains are the nations of the world
sum: Now Hermas asks about the twelve mountains. They are the twelve tribes that live in the whole world, that is, twelve nations, each different in mind and insight, and the Son of God was preached to them by the apostles (94:1-2). Why did the stones of such different mountains all become one bright color in the tower? Because when the nations heard and believed and received the seal, they had one insight, one mind, one faith and one love, and bore the spirits of the virgins with the name (94:3-4). But some defiled themselves after entering, and became worse than before (94:5).
This opens the long explanation of the mountains, one by one, that runs to 106.

views.H: The Amherst papyrus, Lake's introduction says, contains 94:1 and 94:3 (Similitude 9.17.1 and 3), so these verses have a second Greek witness. The witnesses disagree on where the word 'twelve' stands (see the variant).
views.N: The tribes as the church in all the world: James 1:1, Revelation 7:4-9. The repeated 'one' of 94:4 follows Ephesians 4:4-6 (Lake's margin). 'Worse than before': 2 Peter 2:20-22.
views.J: Israel's twelve tribes become the twelve nations of the world. Hermas never mentions Israel here; the old structure of the people of God is simply taken over for the church gathered from the nations.

echoes: James 1:1; Revelation 7:4-9; Ephesians 4:3-6; Colossians 1:23; 2 Peter 2:20-22; Matthew 12:45

settings.what: The explanation of the twelve mountains
settings.by: The Shepherd, the angel of repentance, explaining the parable
settings.to: Hermas, in Arcadia beside the finished tower (78:4), asking question after question
settings.when: After the stones from the deep; the explanation runs mountain by mountain from the black (96:1) to the white (106:1)
settings.why: To hold up twelve kinds of believers as a mirror, from apostates for whom there is no repentance to the childlike who need none, so that each hearer can find himself and act. Most groups are offered repentance with a condition: quickly, before the tower is finished.
settings.readers: Read aloud in the Roman church, the list named sins its members knew: slander and grudges (100), rich members who avoided the poor (97), deacons who stole from widows (103:2), believers who had denied under questioning (103:3-6; 105:4-7).

title: Similitude 9.18: Worse after knowing God; the church made clean
sum: How can people who knew God become worse than before? The Shepherd answers that knowledge raises the stakes: one who does not know God and does evil is punished, but one who has known God and seen his mighty works and still does evil will be punished twice over and will die forever (95:1-2). So the church of God will be made clean. As the rejected stones were thrown out and the tower became like one stone, the church will throw away the evil, the hypocrites, the blasphemers and the double-minded, and be one body, one mind, one faith, one love, and the Son of God will rejoice over his people (95:3-4).

views.N: Luke 12:47-48 (the slave who knew his master's will), Hebrews 10:26-29, 2 Peter 2:21. The purified church: Ephesians 5:27; the parables of the weeds and the net (Matthew 13:24-30, 47-50).
views.D: Hermas pictures a mixed church to be purified before the end, not a church of the pure only. How churches have handled serious sinners in their midst is the subject of the site's cards on church discipline (1 Corinthians 5, Matthew 18).

echoes: Luke 12:47-48; Hebrews 10:26-29; 2 Peter 2:21; Ephesians 5:27; Matthew 13:24-30; Psalm 86:9; Psalm 99:3

title: Similitude 9.19: The black mountain and the bare mountain
sum: The first mountain, the black one, is the apostates, blasphemers against the Lord and betrayers of God's slaves: for them there is no repentance, only death (96:1). The second, the bare mountain, is the hypocrites and teachers of evil, with a name but no faith and no fruit. For them repentance is still there, if they repent quickly (96:2). Why the difference? Because the hypocrites did not blaspheme their Lord or betray his slaves; they taught for gain what sinners wanted to hear, and will pay a penalty, but they may still repent (96:3).

views.N: Hebrews 6:4-6 and 10:26 (no repentance for some), Matthew 12:31-32, 1 John 5:16. Revelation 3:1 ('You have a name for being alive'). 2 Timothy 4:3 and Titus 1:11 on teaching for gain.
views.D: Hermas ranks sins and puts some beyond repentance. The site's cards at Hebrews 6 (falling away) and Matthew 12 (the unforgivable sin) give the churches' answers; the book-level card on repentance after baptism is at 31 (Mandate 4.3).
views.R: Betrayal, handing fellow Christians over to the authorities, was a real danger wherever Christians could be accused before a magistrate; Hermas ranks it with blasphemy (96:1; compare 105:4).

echoes: Hebrews 6:4-6; Hebrews 10:26; Matthew 12:31-32; Revelation 3:1; 2 Timothy 4:3; Titus 1:11; Matthew 10:21

title: Similitude 9.20: The mountain of thorns and thistles: the rich and the busy
sum: The third mountain, with thorns and thistles, is the rich and those tangled up in business. The busy wander off, choked by their affairs; the rich keep their distance from God's slaves for fear of being asked for something. Both will enter the kingdom only with difficulty, as hard as walking barefoot among thistles (97:1-3). But for them there is repentance, a quick one, so that they can make up now for the good they failed to do; if not, they will be handed over to the women in black (97:4).
Three verses here are partly Lake's own Greek, put back from the Latin and Ethiopic where the Athos manuscript skipped words (see the variants at 97:2 and 97:4).

views.N: The seed among thorns (Matthew 13:22; Mark 4:18-19, Lake's margin) and Jesus' 'with difficulty' (Matthew 19:23; Mark 10:23-24; Luke 18:24). James 2:1-6 on favoring the rich.
views.R: In a city church the rich could help or hold back. Hermas's fear is concrete: the rich avoid the poor so as not to be asked for money. Similitude 2 (51) offers the other model: the elm and the vine, each supporting the other.

echoes: Matthew 13:22; Mark 4:18-19; Matthew 19:23-24; Mark 10:23-24; Luke 18:24; Genesis 3:18; James 2:1-6

title: Similitude 9.21: The mountain of half-dry plants: the double-minded
sum: The fourth mountain had plants green at the top and dry at the roots. These are the double-minded and those who have the Lord on their lips but not in their heart. Their words live and their works are dead; they are neither alive nor dead (98:1-2). Like plants that wither in the sun, when they hear of suffering they worship idols out of cowardice and are ashamed of their Lord's name. They can still live if they repent quickly; if not, they are already handed over to the women who take their life (98:3-4).

views.N: James 1:8 (double-minded) and James 2:26 (dead works); Isaiah 29:13 and Matthew 15:8 (lips and heart); the seed scorched by the sun (Matthew 13:6, 21).
views.R: 'When they hear of suffering' points to the test a Christian could face before the authorities: to offer to the gods. Hermas treats it as a known danger, not a story.

echoes: James 1:8; James 2:26; Isaiah 29:13; Matthew 15:8; Matthew 13:6; Matthew 13:20-21; Revelation 3:15-16

title: Similitude 9.22: The rough mountain: believers who know it all
sum: The fifth mountain, green but rough, is believers who are slow to learn, stubborn and pleased with themselves, wanting to know everything and knowing nothing (99:1). Their stubbornness drove out discernment; they praise themselves and want to be self-appointed teachers. Pride emptied many of them, for stubbornness and empty confidence are a great demon. Many were thrown away, but some repented and put themselves under those with discernment. The rest may still repent, for they were foolish rather than evil (99:2-4).

views.H: Lake keeps the Athos manuscript's rare word for 'self-appointed teachers' though the versions seem to read plain 'teachers'; at 99:4 he restores 'foolish' where A seems to read 'most wicked' (see the variants).
views.N: 1 Corinthians 8:2; 1 Timothy 1:7; James 3:1. Lake hears Philippians 2:7-9 in 'emptied while they lifted themselves up'.

echoes: 1 Corinthians 8:1-2; 1 Timothy 1:7; James 3:1; Philippians 2:7-9; Luke 14:11

title: Similitude 9.23: The mountain of cracks: slander and grudges
sum: The sixth mountain had cracks large and small. The small cracks are believers who hold things against one another and wither through slander; many have repented, and the rest will when they hear the commandments (100:1-2). The large cracks are those who keep on slandering and hold grudges; they were thrown out of the tower and will live only with difficulty (100:3). Then the Shepherd turns to the hearers: if God, who rules all, holds no grudge against those who confess, how can a mortal hold one against another? Put away this way of thinking, and the Lord will heal your sins (100:4-5).

views.N: James 4:11-12 (slander, and the one who can save and destroy, Lake's margin), 1 Peter 2:1, Mark 11:25, Matthew 18:23-35.
views.D: Forgiveness of others as the condition of being forgiven, which Hermas presses here and again in 108-110, is shared by all the churches; how God's forgiveness is given is the card at Micah 7.

echoes: James 4:11-12; 1 Peter 2:1; Mark 11:25; Matthew 18:23-35; Leviticus 19:18

settings.what: The angel of repentance appeals to the grudge-holders
settings.by: The Shepherd, naming himself 'the angel of repentance'
settings.to: Inside the story Hermas; in fact the hearers of the book, 'all of you who hold this way of thinking'
settings.when: In the middle of the explanation of the mountains
settings.why: To turn the picture into a call: the Shepherd stops explaining and speaks straight to the church, as he will again at 101:4, 105:5-8 and 108:3-109:5. Knowing who is addressed shows that the parable is aimed at quarrels inside the hearers' own church.

title: Similitude 9.24: The green mountain: the simple and the generous
sum: The seventh mountain was green and thriving, and the more the animals and birds grazed on it, the more it grew. Its believers were always simple, innocent and blessed, holding nothing against one another, rejoicing over God's slaves, clothed in the holy spirit of the virgins, and giving to everyone from their own labor without reproach or hesitation (101:1-2). So the Lord made them grow and gave them favor (101:3). The angel of repentance promises that their descendants will never be wiped out: they are written down among 'our number' and will live with the Son of God (101:4).

views.N: James 1:5 (God gives 'with an open hand and without scolding'), 2 Corinthians 8:2 and 9:11 (simplicity in giving), Luke 10:20 (names written in heaven).
views.D: Two small letters matter here: 'the holy spirit of these virgins' (101:2) and 'his spirit' (101:4). The site writes both lowercase, as Lake does, so as not to decide how Hermas relates the Spirit, the virgins and the Son of God (see the notes, and the chapter pages for 59 and 89).

echoes: James 1:5; 2 Corinthians 9:6-11; Proverbs 11:24-25; Didache 4:7; Luke 10:20; 1 John 4:13

title: Similitude 9.25: The mountain of springs: apostles and teachers
sum: The eighth mountain had many springs, and all the Lord's creation drank from them. Its believers are the apostles and teachers who preached to the whole world and taught the Lord's word with reverence and purity, who kept nothing back for themselves and lived in righteousness and truth, as they had received the Holy Spirit. People like this pass in with the angels.

views.H: Hermas speaks of the apostles and teachers as a finished generation ('who preached', 'who taught'), as he does at 93:5. Lake's introduction dates Pius, under whom the Muratorian Fragment says Hermas wrote, 'about 148 A.D.', notes that 'many critics' think the book was written at intervals over the twenty or thirty years before, and calls the question one 'which can probably never be decided satisfactorily'.
views.N: The verb 'kept back' is the word for Ananias in Acts 5:2-3. The water of the word: Isaiah 55:10-11; John 7:38-39.

echoes: Acts 5:2-3; Titus 2:10; Isaiah 55:10-11; John 7:38-39; Matthew 28:19

title: Similitude 9.26: The desert mountain: deacons who stole, and those who denied
sum: The ninth mountain was a desert full of snakes and wild beasts. Its stained stones are deacons who served badly, robbing widows and orphans and making gain from their ministry; they can live only if they turn and finish their ministry purely (103:1-2). The scabby stones are those who denied their Lord and keep away from God's slaves, like a neglected vine gone wild (103:3-4). For them repentance is possible, unless they denied from the heart; but this is not a license for anyone who plans to deny now, and repentance must come before the tower is finished (103:5-6). The chipped stones are the deceitful and slanderers, whose words kill like the beasts' poison (103:7-8).

views.H: Hermas distinguishes those who denied 'long ago' from anyone who 'is going to deny his Lord now' (103:6). The text implies that some members of the church had denied in the past and were still alive and in reach of the book; it does not say when or where.
views.N: Acts 6:1-6 and 1 Timothy 3:8 (deacons and money), Mark 12:40 and James 1:27 (widows), Hebrews 10:25 (staying away), Matthew 10:33 and 26:75 (denial), Hebrews 6:4-6.
views.D: The time-limited offer of repentance is the book's central teaching: see 6:4-5 (Vision 2), 31:6 (Mandate 4.3) and the topic on repentance. Whether a true believer can fall away for good is the card at Hebrews 6:4-6.
views.R: The deacons of a Roman house church handled money given for the poor. Hermas shows how that trust could be abused (103:2), as he shows good overseers sheltering the needy in 104.

echoes: Acts 6:1-6; 1 Timothy 3:8; Mark 12:40; James 1:27; Hebrews 10:25; Proverbs 24:30-31; Isaiah 5:1-7; Matthew 10:33; Hebrews 6:4-6; James 3:8

settings.what: The terms of repentance for those who denied
settings.to: Hermas, and through him believers who had denied their Lord under questioning
settings.when: Within the explanation of the ninth mountain
settings.why: To open a door for those who denied in the past without opening it for anyone thinking of denying now. Knowing that both groups were in the hearers' church explains the careful wording: 'I do not say this about these present days'.

title: Similitude 9.27: The mountain of sheltering trees: overseers who welcomed guests
sum: The tenth mountain had trees sheltering some sheep. Its believers are overseers and people who welcome guests, who gladly took God's slaves into their homes without pretense, and overseers who by their ministry always sheltered the needy and the widows and lived in purity. The Lord will shelter them forever; they are glorious in God's sight, and their place is already with the angels, if they go on serving the Lord to the end.

views.H: Hermas speaks of overseers in the plural (104:2; compare 13:1) and of the elders who lead the church (8:3), without saying whether one overseer stood above the others in Rome.
views.N: Overseers who are 'welcoming to strangers': 1 Timothy 3:2; Titus 1:8. Hospitality: Romans 12:13; Hebrews 13:2; 3 John 5-8.
views.D: The site's cards on bishops and elders (Philippians 1:1, Acts 20:28, 1 Timothy 3, Titus 1) set out how the churches read the early evidence. Hermas is one more witness: several overseers, praised for care of the poor, beside elders and deacons.
views.R: In Rome travelling Christians needed lodging, and a house church was a home. The overseers' 'ministry' of sheltering widows and the needy was practical: food and roof.

deep.b:
Greek episkopoi kai philoxenoi: 'overseers and people who welcome guests'. The site renders episkopos 'overseer' in every early Christian writing, with the gloss 'the word behind "bishop"', so that the reader can see the same word in Philippians 1:1 and here, and decide when it became a single office.

What the text shows: (1) the overseers are plural; (2) they are known for hospitality and for sheltering widows and the needy 'by their ministry' (diakonia); (3) they are set among the believers of one mountain, not over the whole tower; (4) elsewhere in the book they stand with apostles, teachers and deacons (13:1), and the church in Rome is led by elders (8:3). What it does not show: whether the overseers and the elders were the same people, and whether one of them presided.

The deacons of 103:2, who robbed the widows, are the opposite picture. Between them, chapters 103-104 show the church's money and its care for the weak passing through the hands of its officers, and Hermas judging them by how they used it.

echoes: 1 Timothy 3:2; Titus 1:7-8; Philippians 1:1; Acts 20:28; Romans 12:13; Hebrews 13:2; 3 John 5-8; 1 Peter 4:9

title: Similitude 9.28: The mountain of fruit trees: those who suffered for the name
sum: The eleventh mountain had trees full of fruit of different kinds. Its believers suffered for the name of the Son of God, eagerly and with their whole heart, and gave up their lives; all their sins were taken away (105:1-3). Those who did not deny when brought before the authorities have the better fruit; those who wavered and debated whether to deny, and then suffered, have less, because the evil plan that a slave should deny his own master came into their hearts (105:4). The Shepherd then speaks to the hearers: give glory to God if you suffer for the name, and confess that you have a Lord (105:5-8).

views.N: Acts 15:26 (Lake's margin), 1 Peter 4:13-16, Matthew 5:11-12 and Luke 6:22 (Lake's margin), Matthew 10:32-33.
views.D: That suffering for the name took away sins (105:3) became, in later writers, the 'baptism of blood' (Tertullian, On Baptism 16; Catechism of the Catholic Church 1258). Whether the sufferings of the faithful can atone is the card at 2 Maccabees 7.
views.R: Christians 'brought before the authorities and questioned' (105:4) faced a Roman magistrate; slaves who denied their masters were punished (105:8), a picture every hearer in Rome understood.

echoes: Acts 15:26; 1 Peter 4:13-16; Matthew 5:11-12; Luke 6:22; Matthew 10:32-33; Luke 12:11-12; Revelation 2:13

settings.what: A word to those who suffer and those who waver
settings.to: Two groups among the hearers: 'you who are planning this' (to deny) and 'you who suffer for the name'
settings.when: After the explanation of the eleventh mountain
settings.why: To steady those facing trial and to warn the waverers with an argument from Roman slavery: a master punishes a slave who disowns him, so what will the Lord of all do?

title: Similitude 9.29: The white mountain: those like babies
sum: The twelfth mountain, the white one, is believers like little babies, into whose hearts no evil comes, who never knew wickedness and stayed childlike all their lives. They will live in the kingdom of God without doubt, because they never defiled God's commandments (106:1-2). All who become like babies will be more glorious than all the rest, for babies are glorious and first in God's sight (106:3). With the mountains finished, Hermas asks about the stones from the plain and the round stones (106:4).

views.N: Matthew 18:3 (Lake's margin) and 19:14; 1 Peter 2:2; Ephesians 4:22-24 (take off, put on).
views.D: Hermas's ideal of childlike innocence is the theme of Mandate 2 (27:1). No repentance is mentioned for the white mountain, as for several of the good mountains (101; 102; 104; 105).

echoes: Matthew 18:3-4; Matthew 19:14; 1 Peter 2:2; 1 Corinthians 14:20; Ephesians 4:22-24; Colossians 3:12

settings.what: The stones from the plain, the round stones, and the last appeal
settings.by: The Shepherd, the angel of repentance, explaining the parable
settings.to: Hermas, in Arcadia beside the finished tower (78:4), asking question after question
settings.when: After the twelve mountains (106:4); from 107:3 the text survives in Latin
settings.why: To finish the parable: the stones from the plain and the round stones are innocent believers, some held back by wealth. The explanation turns into the Shepherd's last appeal to the church (108:3-110:1): keep simplicity, forget wrongs, heal splits, and repent while the tower is still being built.

title: Similitude 9.30: The roots of the white mountain and the round stones (from 107:3 the Latin)
sum: This chapter rests on two witnesses: its first two verses are the last of the Athos manuscript, and from 107:3 the Plain English Translation follows Lake's Latin, with a few lines of the Amherst papyrus. The stones from the plain are the roots of the white mountain: innocent people who could go into the tower without making it dirty (107:1-3). The round, bright stones are from the white mountain too. Their riches dimmed them a little from the truth, but they never left God, so the Lord ordered their wealth cut back, not taken away, so that they could do good with what was left (107:4-5).

views.H: At 107:2 'A ends, as the last leaf is missing' (Lake). From 107:3 Lake prints the Vulgate Latin (L1), with Greek where it survives: here 107:3-4 from the Amherst papyrus, which Lake says is 'in bad condition' but restored with reconstructions that 'are almost certain'.
views.N: Riches and the kingdom: Mark 10:23; 1 Timothy 6:17-19. Roots and branches: Romans 11:16-18.
views.R: The round stones are the rich of the Roman church. Vision 3 (14:5-6) says their wealth must be 'cut away'; here it is cut back only in part, so that they keep enough to give.

deep.b:
The Athos manuscript (A), copied in the 1400s and the only continuous Greek for most of the book, has lost its last leaf. Lake's footnote at 107:2: 'At this point A ends, as the last leaf is missing. The Latin text which follows is that of L1.' L1 is the Vulgate Latin, 'found in many MSS., published in the Editio Princeps of Faber, Paris, 1513'; L2 is the Palatine Latin (Lake's introduction).

From 107:3 to 114:5 Lake prints L1, and sets into it the few Greek lines that survive: 107:3-4 from the Amherst papyrus, 108:5-6 from a quotation in Antiochus of Palestine, and 113:3-5 from Oxyrhynchus Papyrus 404. In five verses (107:3, 107:4, 108:6, 113:3, 113:5) the language changes in the middle; each has a variant entry naming the witness for each half. Where Lake's footnotes give a reading of L2 (109:3) or a scholar's correction (112:4), the variants give it.

For the reader this means that 27 verses are a translation of a translation: Hermas wrote Greek, an early translator made it Latin, and the Plain English Translation makes the Latin English. The notes give the Latin word wherever the sense turns on it. Crombie's English in the Ante-Nicene Fathers, used here for checking, translates the Latin too.

echoes: Mark 10:23; 1 Timothy 6:17-19; Romans 11:16-18; Isaiah 11:1

title: Similitude 9.31: Round stones still waiting, and the shepherds who must answer
sum: The text of this chapter rests on Lake's Latin (L1), except 108:5-6, which he prints from a Greek quotation in Antiochus. The round stones that were not yet fitted into the building have not yet received the seal; they are put back in their place until this world and the empty show of their riches are cut away from them, and then they will fit into God's kingdom, for the Lord has blessed this innocent kind (108:1-2). The angel of repentance blesses all who are innocent like babies (108:3) and charges all who have the seal: keep simplicity, do not keep the memory of wrongs, heal the splits among you, so that the Lord of the flocks may be glad (108:4). Woe to the shepherds if any sheep are lost; and if the shepherds themselves fall away, they cannot blame the sheep. The Shepherd too must give account (108:5-6).

views.H: For 108:5-6 Lake prints the Greek of a quotation in Antiochus of Palestine; the end of 108:6 and the rest of the chapter are Latin. Lake gives no Latin for the Greek part, so the variant at 108:6 names the witness for each half.
views.N: Ezekiel 34 (the bad shepherds), 1 Peter 5:2-4, Hebrews 13:17 ('as people who must give an account'), 1 Corinthians 1:10 (no splits).
views.D: The shepherds of 108:5-6 are the church's leaders, held responsible for the flock. The site's cards on church order (Acts 20:28, 1 Timothy 3) give the churches' views of those offices.

echoes: Ezekiel 34:1-10; 1 Peter 5:2-4; Hebrews 13:17; John 10:11; 1 Corinthians 1:10; Luke 15:4-7

settings.what: The angel of repentance's charge to the church and its shepherds
settings.to: All 'who have received this seal', and their shepherds, the leaders of the church
settings.when: At the end of the explanation of the stones, as the parable turns into exhortation; the text is Latin with two Greek verses
settings.why: To heal a divided church: forget wrongs, remove the splits, and remember that leaders answer for every lost sheep. Read with 100 (grudges) and 103:2 (deacons), it shows that Hermas's church had quarrels among members and failures among officers.

title: Similitude 9.32: Give back the spirit whole: the torn garment
sum: The text of this chapter rests on Lake's Latin (L1). Heal yourselves while the tower is still being built. The Lord lives among those who love peace and keeps far from the quarrelsome, so give back to him whole the spirit you received (109:1-2). If you gave a fuller a new garment and he returned it torn, you would be furious; what then will the Lord do to you, who gave you the spirit whole and have made it useless? He will punish you with death (109:3-4). Hermas agrees that he will punish all who hold on to the memory of wrongs. The Shepherd ends: do not trample on his kindness, for he is patient with your sins and not like you; repent (109:5).

views.H: Lake's footnote: much of this chapter survives in Greek in Antiochus, but 'he seems here to abbreviate and perhaps to paraphrase too much to render it wise to follow his text', so Lake prints only the Latin. The Palatine Latin has 'be angry' for the Vulgate Latin's 'flare up' (109:3).
views.N: 1 Thessalonians 5:23 (spirit kept whole), Ephesians 4:30 (grieving the Spirit), Romans 2:4 (God's patience), Matthew 18:32-35.
views.R: A fuller washed, bleached and finished cloth (compare Mark 9:3). Hermas's picture assumes his hearers had all handed a garment to one and wanted it back whole.

echoes: 1 Thessalonians 5:23; Ephesians 4:30; Romans 2:4; Matthew 18:32-35; Mark 9:3; 28:2

title: Similitude 9.33: The marks smoothed over
sum: The text of this chapter rests on Lake's Latin (L1). The Shepherd closes his teaching: all that is written above he, the angel of repentance, has shown to God's slaves. Believe, listen, walk in his words and set your paths straight, and you will live; stay in wickedness and the memory of wrongs, and no one of that kind will live to God (110:1). Then he asks Hermas why he did not ask about the marks on the stones, which they had filled in. Hermas forgot. The marks were the sins of those who repented with all their hearts, and the Lord had them wiped out and smoothed level so that they would not show (110:2-3).

views.N: Acts 3:19 (sins wiped away), Isaiah 43:25, Psalm 103:12.
views.D: The filled-in marks are the book's picture of forgiveness after repentance: the sins are not only pardoned but made invisible in the building.

echoes: Acts 3:19; Isaiah 43:25; Psalm 103:12; Micah 7:19; Deuteronomy 30:15-20

title: Similitude 10.1: The angel's last charge: Hermas handed over to the Shepherd
sum: Similitude 10 is the book's ending, and it rests on the Latin (with Greek again in 113:3-5). After Hermas finishes writing the book, the angel who had handed him over to the Shepherd comes to his house, sits on the couch, and the Shepherd stands at his right (111:1). The angel tells Hermas that he and his house are in the Shepherd's care, and that if he walks in the commandments he will master all wickedness and every desire of the world (111:2-3). He tells Hermas to say to everyone that the Shepherd has great honor and power with the Lord: to him alone in the whole world the power of repentance has been given (111:3).

views.H: Lake's Latin has 'which I gave you' (quae dedi tibi) in 111:2, though his English says 'which he gave you' (see the variant and the note).
views.J: An angel over repentance with a higher angel above him belongs to the book's ranks of angels; it names Michael as the great angel over God's people in 69:3, as Daniel 12:1 does. Who the angel of Similitude 10 is, the text does not say.
views.D: The Shepherd's 'power of repentance' (111:3) is not the power to forgive, which the Gospels give the Son of Man (Mark 2:10). Who the Shepherd and the higher angel are, and how they relate to the Son of God, is set out on the chapter pages for 25 and 89.

echoes: Mark 2:10; John 20:23; Daniel 12:1; Acts 5:31

settings.by: The angel who had handed Hermas over to the Shepherd (25:2, the most revered angel)
settings.to: Hermas, in the house where he is staying, with the Shepherd standing by
settings.when: After Hermas has finished writing the book (111:1)
settings.why: To seal the book: to confirm the Shepherd's authority, to give Hermas his ministry of telling everyone the great things of the Lord, to leave the virgins with him, and to end with the warning that the tower will soon be finished.
settings.readers: The book's hearers in Rome are addressed directly at the end ('Tell everyone', 114:2; 'all of you who have received from the Lord', 114:4): the farewell turns Hermas's private vision into a public charge.

title: Similitude 10.2: Hermas's ministry
sum: The text of this chapter rests on Lake's Latin (L1). Hermas asks the angel to ask the Shepherd whether he has done anything wrong since the Shepherd came into his house. The angel knows he has not, and speaks so that Hermas will keep going, and tell these words to others, so that those who repent will think as he does (112:1-2). Hermas says he tells everyone the great things of the Lord and hopes sinners will repent and get their life back (112:3). The angel charges him to finish this ministry: those who keep the Shepherd's commandments will have life, and those who do not run from their own life and are guilty of their own blood (112:4).

views.H: Lake notes Hilgenfeld's correction 'aversantur illum' for the Latin 'illum adversus' (112:4); the Plain English Translation keeps the Latin.
views.N: Acts 2:11 (the great things of God, Lake's margin); Acts 18:6 and Ezekiel 3:18-19 (one's own blood).

echoes: Acts 2:11; Acts 18:6; Ezekiel 3:18-19; Ezekiel 33:4-6

title: Similitude 10.3: The virgins stay with Hermas
sum: The text of this chapter rests on Lake's Latin (L1), except the Greek of Oxyrhynchus Papyrus 404 in 113:3-5. The angel has sent the virgins to live with Hermas as helpers, for the commandments cannot be kept without them. They will stay as long as his house is clean, and leave at the first uncleanness (113:1-2). Hermas hopes to please them, as he has pleased the Shepherd (113:3). The angel tells the Shepherd that God's slave wants to live and will keep the commandments, hands Hermas back to the Shepherd, and entrusts Hermas and his house to the virgins, who gladly agree (113:4-5). From the middle of 113:3 to the middle of 113:5 Lake prints the Greek of Oxyrhynchus Papyrus 404.

views.H: Oxyrhynchus Papyrus 404, published by Grenfell and Hunt in Oxyrhynchus Papyri iii (Lake's introduction), has a gap after 'calling the virgins' (113:5).
views.N: Matthew 12:43-45 (the swept house), 1 Corinthians 6:19 (the body a temple of the Spirit), John 14:23.
views.D: The commandments cannot be kept without the virgins, the powers of the Son of God (90:2). Christian traditions explain the relation of grace and obedience differently; the cards on faith and works (Romans 3, James 2) give their answers.

echoes: Matthew 12:43-45; 1 Corinthians 6:19; John 14:23; Ezekiel 36:27

title: Similitude 10.4: Do good before the tower is finished
sum: The text of this chapter rests on Lake's Latin (L1). The angel's last words: carry yourself bravely in this ministry and tell everyone the great things of the Lord (114:1). Tell all who can do good not to stop, for everyone must be rescued from hardship; the person in need suffers like one in chains, and many in such distress bring death on themselves. Whoever knows of it and does not help is guilty of that person's blood (114:2-3). Do good works, all of you who have received from the Lord, before the tower is finished, for the building has been paused for your sake; if you do not hurry, you will be shut out (114:4). Then the angel rises, takes the Shepherd and the virgins, and goes, promising to send them back to Hermas's house (114:5).

views.H: The book ends in Latin, with no closing blessing; Crombie's English in the Ante-Nicene Fathers adds 'Amen', which Lake's Latin does not have.
views.N: Ezekiel 3:18 and Proverbs 24:11-12 (guilty for not rescuing), 1 John 3:17, Galatians 6:9-10, 2 Peter 3:9 (the delay for repentance).
views.R: Hermas's last command is practical charity in a city where the poor could fall into 'great torment and distress' (114:2), and he names the deaths such distress caused.

echoes: Ezekiel 3:18; Proverbs 24:11-12; 1 John 3:17; Galatians 6:9-10; 2 Peter 3:9; Matthew 25:10-12
